## 3.1.2. Arsenic

## 3.1.

Toxic elements

## 3.1.1. Aluminum

The range of values for aluminum in white rice was 6.1023.4 mg/kg while the range for brown rice was 7.40-43.0 mg/kg. The mean values for white and brown rice were 9.30 and 14.7 mg/ kg, respectively. The maximum value of 43.0 mg/kg was found in the brown basmati rice brand. The bulk rice had 23.4 mg/kg and a brand of long grained parboiled rice had 15.6 mg/kg. A diet high in rice would not be expected to expose humans to toxic levels of aluminum, but it is of note that the preference in the Jamaican diet is bulk rice which has the second highest quantity of Al in the survey. Aluminum has not been shown to perform any essential function in humans (McDowell, 1992). There has been growing evidence of toxicity however and the World Health Organization revised the Provisional Tolerable Weekly Intake (PTWI) from 7 mg/ kg of body weight to 1 mg/kg of body weight in 2006 based on the conclusions that levels lower than the previous PTWI (Provisional Tolerable Weekly Intake) may affect the developing nervous and reproductive systems (JECFA, 2007). There have been several studies linking an accumulation of aluminum in the brain and Alzheimer's disease but no causal relationship has as yet been established (Frisardi et al., 2010).

The arsenic content of the white rice samples had a range of 0.110-0.487 mg/kg, while the range for brown rice was 0.0820.250 mg/kg. The mean arsenic content of the white rice samples was 0.20 mg/kg, and 0.165 mg/kg for brown rice. The highest sample measured, Roland Arborio rice from Italy, contained 0.49 mg/kg of arsenic. The likely source of arsenic is the water with which the paddies are flooded. Some arsenic compounds are used in herbicides and fungicides. A limit for arsenic in rice has not been established by CODEX; however the WHO has established a PTWI of 0.015 mg/kg bw for inorganic arsenic. Chronic arsenic overexposure results in clinical manifestations in almost every system of the body.

Arsenic in groundwater has been well publicized because of the elevated levels found in some countries (Chowdhury et al., 2000). Arsenic in foods occurs predominantly as non-toxic arsenobetaine and arsenocholine which are excreted unchanged from the human body (Ratnaike, 2003). The origin of rice may affect the dominant form of arsenic present and it appears that rice from the United States of America has more dimethyl arsenic acid which may be less of a health risk than rice from Asia and Europe which may have more inorganic arsenic (Zavala et al., 2008).

All samples were ground to a fine powder for analysis using a Fritsch Pulverisette 2 automated agate mortar and pestle (Fritsch, Germany). Samples were prepared for analysis by ICP-OES, F-AAS and TXRF by acid digestion. 20 mL of 1:3 HCl:HNO3 (Fisher TraceMetal Grade acids; Fisher Chemical, MA, USA) was added to 1 g of sample in a 70 mL graduated polyethylene vial, covered with a polyethylene watch glass and allowed to stand overnight. The following day the samples were digested at 110 8 C for 2 h using a graphite heating block (ModBlock; CPI International, CA, USA) and made up to 50 mL with 2% HNO3 (Howe et al., 2005).

The analytical techniques used were flame atomic absorption spectrophotometry (F-AAS) using a PerkinElmer 5100PC Spectrophotometer (PerkinElmer, MA, USA); inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) using a PerkinElmer Optima 7000DV (PerkinElmer, MA, USA); instrumental neutron activation analysis (INAA) using a SLOWPOKE II research reactor (Atomic Energy of Canada Limited, ON, Canada); and total reflection X-ray fluorescence (TXRF) using a Wobistrax /C223 TXRF spectrometer (Atominstitut der O ¨ sterreichischen Universita ¨ten, Vienna University of Technology, Vienna, Austria). The technique selected for each element was dependent on availability at the institution, detection limit and robustness.

Measurements by AAS and ICP-OES were done in triplicate, with the mean results being presented. The uncertainty of the measurements by INAA and TXRF are a function of acquisition time.

Calibration standards for F-AAS and ICP-OES analyses were prepared using Certiprep solutions (SPEX Certiprep, NJ, USA) in 2% HNO3. Deuterium lamp background corrections were performed for AAS. An internal standard containing 0.04 mg/L scandium and 0.2 mg/L yttrium was used for ICP-OES analyses.

For analyses using TXRF, the calibration and internal standards were prepared by serial dilutions of a solution containing 10,000 mg/L (Certiprep solutions) in 5% HNO3. An aliquot of a cobalt (Co) solution was added as an internal standard to achieve a final concentration of 10 mg/L. The samples were then homogenized with a vortex mixer and analyzed after pipetting 10 m L onto a quartz sample carrier/reflector and evaporating the solvent on a hot plate at low power.

The samples were irradiated under vacuum for 1000 s at 50 kV and 40 mA in a Wobistrax /C223 TXRF spectrometer (Streli et al., 2004). Blanks were treated identically to the samples.

Each sample was irradiated for 3 min at a neutron flux of 5 /C2 10 11 n cm /C0 2 s /C0 1 and allowed decay periods of approximately 5 and 60 min before counting. ## 1. Introduction

Rice ( Oryza sativa ) is a widely consumed staple in Jamaica (Samuda et al., 1998a,b), and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) lists Jamaica among the countries that are significant per capita consumers of rice (Kennedy et al., 2002). Both plain rice and rice and peas were ranked among the top 10 most consumed foods in the country with rice being the only starch staple in the top 10. Although cooked rice and peas (composite sample from several Jamaican households) has been analyzed for some nutrients by the Caribbean Food and Nutrition Institute (Samuda et al., 1998b), plain rice was not analyzed and was found to be more popularly consumed in the Kingston Metropolitan Area where 28% of Jamaica's population lives; there has been no comprehensive elemental analysis of this predominant staple of the Jamaican population.

Large-scale, local cultivation of rice has been discontinued for more than two decades and the rice now available on the market is all imported. Some 44,882 metric tonnes of this (termed ''bulk rice'', which is polished white rice packaged without branding) was imported from Guyana in 2009 accounting for 57% of rice imports.

* Corresponding author.

Tel.: +876 935 8532-3; fax: +876 977 0768. E-mail address: leslie.hoofung@uwimona.edu.jm (L.A. Hoo Fung).

Another 25,266 tonnes was imported from the United States of America (JIS, 2010). In an effort to reduce the dependence on foreign supply of this important staple and consequently to lower the food import bill there has been a recent push to reintroduce farmers to rice cultivation.

A burgeoning health consciousness in some sectors of the public has seen a greater availability of brown rice on the Jamaican market. The fiber and higher vitamins and minerals as a result of the retention of the bran have increased the popularity of this version of the commodity. In addition, parboiled and/or enriched white rice is also available and these methods of processing can be expected to affect the elemental profile of white rice.

Food security is of growing global concern.

These concerns include the reliability of supply and the quality of food. Food composition data is necessary when estimating a population's intake of nutrients and dietary exposure to toxins and indeed, assessing diet quality. This paper examines the elemental content of rice available on the market and therefore, its contribution to the Jamaican public's nutrition. Some Jamaican soils are naturally enriched in toxic elements such as arsenic, cadmium and mercury (Lalor et al., 1999). If local rice cultivation is to resume, it is vital that the uptake of toxic elements and nutrients is assessed. The analysis of locally grown rice from field trials allows preliminary estimates to be made toward achieving this objective.

## 2. Methodology

Commercially available rice samples were purchased from supermarkets in the parish of St.

Andrew, Jamaica in February 2010. This parish was ideal for sampling as a significant portion of the Jamaican population resides there. While bulk rice is readily available across the island, other rice brands sampled are typically not sold outside the Kingston Metropolitan Area (which includes the parishes of Kingston and St. Andrew), and indeed the other brands of rice available on the market change from time to time but were representative of the brands available at the time of sampling. A minimum of 500 g of each rice brand was collected. A composite sample of locally grown rice produced in the parish of St. Catherine was also obtained from the Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries.

## 3.1.

Toxic elements

## 3.1.1. Aluminum

The range of values for aluminum in white rice was 6.1023.4 mg/kg while the range for brown rice was 7.40-43.0 mg/kg. The mean values for white and brown rice were 9.30 and 14.7 mg/ kg, respectively. The maximum value of 43.0 mg/kg was found in the brown basmati rice brand. The bulk rice had 23.4 mg/kg and a brand of long grained parboiled rice had 15.6 mg/kg. A diet high in rice would not be expected to expose humans to toxic levels of aluminum, but it is of note that the preference in the Jamaican diet is bulk rice which has the second highest quantity of Al in the survey. Aluminum has not been shown to perform any essential function in humans (McDowell, 1992). There has been growing evidence of toxicity however and the World Health Organization revised the Provisional Tolerable Weekly Intake (PTWI) from 7 mg/ kg of body weight to 1 mg/kg of body weight in 2006 based on the conclusions that levels lower than the previous PTWI (Provisional Tolerable Weekly Intake) may affect the developing nervous and reproductive systems (JECFA, 2007). There have been several studies linking an accumulation of aluminum in the brain and Alzheimer's disease but no causal relationship has as yet been established (Frisardi et al., 2010).

The arsenic content of the white rice samples had a range of 0.110-0.487 mg/kg, while the range for brown rice was 0.0820.250 mg/kg. The mean arsenic content of the white rice samples was 0.20 mg/kg, and 0.165 mg/kg for brown rice. The highest sample measured, Roland Arborio rice from Italy, contained 0.49 mg/kg of arsenic. The likely source of arsenic is the water with which the paddies are flooded. Some arsenic compounds are used in herbicides and fungicides. A limit for arsenic in rice has not been established by CODEX; however the WHO has established a PTWI of 0.015 mg/kg bw for inorganic arsenic. Chronic arsenic overexposure results in clinical manifestations in almost every system of the body.

Arsenic in groundwater has been well publicized because of the elevated levels found in some countries (Chowdhury et al., 2000). Arsenic in foods occurs predominantly as non-toxic arsenobetaine and arsenocholine which are excreted unchanged from the human body (Ratnaike, 2003). The origin of rice may affect the dominant form of arsenic present and it appears that rice from the United States of America has more dimethyl arsenic acid which may be less of a health risk than rice from Asia and Europe which may have more inorganic arsenic (Zavala et al., 2008).

## 3.2.2. Cobalt

The cobalt concentration ranged from 0.073 to 0.132 mg/kg for white rice and 0.081 to 0.136 mg/kg for brown rice.

The mean concentration was found to be 0.097 mg/kg in white rice and 0.105 mg/kg in brown rice. Cobalt is an essential trace nutrient, particularly as a constituent of vitamin B12 and some metalloproteins. As it is present in small amounts in most foods deficiency is rare; a lack however may lead to pernicious anemia which can be fatal (McDowell, 1992).

## 3.2.3. Chromium

The chromium content of the white rice samples ranged from < 0.030 to 0.159 mg/kg; the range for brown rice samples was < 0.030-0.487 mg/kg. Humans require chromium in trace amounts. Its mechanisms in the body are not well defined but it is known to enhance the action of insulin, and appears to aid in the metabolism and storage of protein, carbohydrates and fats.

## 3.2.4. Copper

The copper concentration of white rice samples ranged from < 0.770 to 2.72 mg/kg and the brown rice samples from 1.60 to 4.74 mg/kg. The mean concentration found in white rice was 1.65 mg/kg; in brown rice the mean was 2.96 mg/kg. Copper is essential to humans in small quantities as a key component of redox enzymes and hemocyanin; it is involved in mitochondrial function, cellular metabolism, connective tissue formation, and the absorption, storage and metabolism of iron (NIH). The copper content of rice varies greatly with different cultivars (Yan et al., 2006) and so this could be a function of the variety selected for the local field trials.

lists iron deficiency as the 6th leading cause of illness and disease in low income countries.

There are several recognized factors related to this deficiency; low bioavailability of iron in foods, inability to meet iron demand during growth spurts such as infancy and pregnancy, blood loss in women of childbearing age through menstruation and childbirth, blood losses from parasitic infections and loss from diseases like malaria. Most of the iron in the body is found in heme proteins such as hemoglobin and myoglobin, both involved in oxygen transport. Iron is also found as a constituent of heme enzymes such as cytochromes, catalases and peroxidizes and other non heme compounds (McDowell, 1992). The amount of bioavailable iron in rice and other staple plants is low, and the phytic acid present in rice may add to this lack of bioavailability (Glahn et al., 2002). This is a likely contributor to the global iron deficiency problem. The polishing of rice may remove phytic acid and polyphenols, and enrichment may be an important tool in combating iron deficiency (Liang, 2007).

Magnesium concentrations in white rice ranged from 176 to 562 mg/kg, and 340 to 1450 mg/kg in brown rice.

## 3.1.4. Mercury

The average mercury content of the white rice samples ranged from < 0.015 to < 0.085 mg/kg while the range for brown rice was < 0.024 to < 0.112 mg/kg. Mercury has no known essentiality in humans and the toxic effects of mercury compounds and in particular methylmercury are well known.

Methylmercury poisoning through the ingestion of fish from industrially contaminated waters was the cause of mass poisoning in Minamata, Japan (Ekino et al., 2007). The symptoms of mercury poisoning range from the neurological to the renal, reproductive and cardiovascular systems and its effect on the nervous system of the developing fetus have been described (McDowell, 1992; Berry, 2008).

The calcium content of Zatarain's Parboiled was significantly higher than other samples at 425 mg/kg. deficiency in animals and humans however, is well known and described in literature. Symptoms range from growth retardation, nausea, muscle weakness, tetany and this deficiency may affect cardiac function (McDowell, 1992). It was thought the typical westernized diet provided adequate magnesium; however a significant amount of the US population may be falling short of recommended intake amounts (Rude, 1998). This may suggest that a tendency toward deficiency is more likely than previously estimated. According to the NIH, a cup of cooked brown rice contains approximately 80 mg of magnesium, which would be about 20% of RDA.

## 3.2.7. Manganese

The manganese concentrations in white rice samples ranged from 5.02 to 17.1 mg/kg; the range for brown rice was 5.1943.5 mg/kg. The mean concentration of manganese in the white rice samples analyzed was 10.5 mg/kg and 26.5 mg/kg in brown rice samples, with Roland Black Japonica rice having the highest levels. Brown rice is known as a good source of manganese and several of the samples had manganese levels in excess of 30 mg/ kg. Manganese is essential to human beings. It can function as an enzyme activator for several enzymes and as a component of some metalloenzymes.

It is also important for bone growth, carbohydrate and lipid metabolism. Because of its ubiquity in foods, deficiency is unlikely in an adequate diet. Its toxicity, however, is also well documented, but is unlikely from dietary exposure except under special circumstances (McDowell, 1992; Crossgrove and Zheng, 2004). Although there is no established recommended daily allowance for manganese it is estimated that adult males and females require 2.3 and 1.8 mg per day respectively. An upper limit of 11 mg per day for adults has been determined (NIH).

## 3.2.8. Molybdenum

The range of molybdenum values found in white rice samples was 0.438-1.62 mg/kg and the range for brown rice samples was 0.447-1.20 mg/kg. The mean values for white rice and brown rice were 0.790 and 0.770 mg/kg respectively. The highest value was found in the Mahatma long grain enriched rice. The bulk rice most consumed by Jamaicans had a value of 0.48 mg/kg. Molybdenum is an essential trace nutrient.

In humans it plays an important role in the regulation of calcium, magnesium and copper metabolism. It is biologically active as a co factor to several enzymes as well as the oxidation of sulfite and the formation of uric acid (McDowell, 1992). Because of the relatively low daily requirements of this nutrient (RDA, 45 m g/day for adults) and high tolerance (up to 10 mg/day) deficiency and toxicity from balanced dietary intake is unlikely.

## 3.2.9. Phosphorus

Phosphorus in the white rice samples ranged from 335 to 2591 mg/kg, and from 931 to 4339 mg/kg in brown rice.

The mean total phosphorus in the white rice samples analyzed was 1203 mg/ kg; the mean in the brown rice samples was 3361 mg/kg. Not surprisingly the highest result overall was obtained in a sample of brown rice. Also of note is the black japonica variety, which was found to contain 4137 mg/kg of phosphorus. Several brands of brown rice were found to have levels closer to the maximum value observed in this study.

Phosphorus, as phosphates, is among the most abundant of mineral elements in the human body. Deficiencies in phosphorus nutrition have historically been seen in rickets and osteomalacia (which may also be caused by an inadequacy in calcium and/or vitamin D) as well as other bone symptoms and skeletal deformities. It does not appear that the typical adult diet is deficient in phosphorus. Of great importance is the presence of phosphorus in its storage form phytic acid. Phytic acid is considered an anti-nutrient because of its binding affinity for several elements of nutritional consequence such as iron, zinc and calcium. About 80% of phosphorus in rice is stored as phytic acid (Mohammed, 2008).

## 3.2.2. Cobalt

The cobalt concentration ranged from 0.073 to 0.132 mg/kg for white rice and 0.081 to 0.136 mg/kg for brown rice.

The mean concentration was found to be 0.097 mg/kg in white rice and 0.105 mg/kg in brown rice. Cobalt is an essential trace nutrient, particularly as a constituent of vitamin B12 and some metalloproteins. As it is present in small amounts in most foods deficiency is rare; a lack however may lead to pernicious anemia which can be fatal (McDowell, 1992).

## 3.2.3. Chromium

The chromium content of the white rice samples ranged from < 0.030 to 0.159 mg/kg; the range for brown rice samples was < 0.030-0.487 mg/kg. The mean chromium content of the white rice samples was 0.080 mg/kg and the mean for brown rice was 0.157 mg/kg. The highest value, 0.487 mg/kg, was found in Three Jewels Brown Rice. Humans require chromium in trace amounts. Its mechanisms in the body are not well defined but it is known to enhance the action of insulin, and appears to aid in the metabolism and storage of protein, carbohydrates and fats.

Chromium is present in very low levels in food and absorption rates in the body are low, between 0.4% and 2.5%. It is primarily found in two forms: Cr(III), which is biologically active, and Cr(VI),

About 80% of phosphorus in rice is stored as phytic acid (Mohammed, 2008). About 50% of the mineral content is retained in the bran. This is removed when polishing rice. It is for this reason that brown rice would have more phosphorus and consequently more phytic acid. In cases where rice is an important source of calories the already low mineral content may be further reduced by the relatively high levels of phytic acid.

## 3.2.10. Potassium

The potassium content of white rice samples was found to range from 465 to 1659 mg/kg while the range for brown rice samples was 833-3097 mg/kg. The mean for white rice was 913 mg/kg and 2157 mg/kg for brown rice. The average for white rice content is somewhat lower than that quoted in other publications while the mean for brown rice was similar (Mohammed and Spyrou, 2009; Phuong et al., 1999). Roland Black Japonica rice had the highest concentration of potassium while the lowest concentration was found in Mahatma Jasmine rice. Potassium is the third most abundant mineral in the human body and is essential to human life.

Potassium is the dominant intracellular cation and functions as a regulator in the acid-base and the osmotic balance of the cell. Potassium plays an important role in muscle contraction and nerve impulse transmission through the movement of potassium and sodium ions across voltage gated ion channels during action potential. Potassium is also known as a cofactor in many enzymes involved in protein synthesis, energy transfer and the storage of carbohydrates for use as fuel in muscles (McDowell, 1992; Schmidt-Nielsen, 1997).

## 3.2.11. Selenium

Selenium values for white rice ranged from < 0.028 to 0.236 mg/ kg and those for brown rice from < 0.058 to 0.204 mg/kg. Seventysix percent of the samples had detectable levels of selenium with a mean value of 0.108 mg/kg in white rice and 0.131 mg/kg in brown rice.

It has been shown that staples grown in soils with high Se bioavailability will have relatively high selenium content, with the converse being the case in soils with low selenium content (IPCS, 1987). The ability of selenium to bind toxic heavy metals, especially mercury, mitigates its various pathological effects, especially those related to the brain of the developing fetus, has been known for some time if not always highlighted in studies on risk of mercury exposure (Berry, 2008).

## 3.2.12. Sodium

The sodium content of the white rice samples had a range of 1.65-11.4 mg/kg while the brown rice samples ranged from 5.07 to 48.1 mg/kg. The mean concentration of sodium in the white rice samples was 6.00 mg/kg; the mean for brown rice is 15.1 mg/kg. The highest sodium was found in Uncle Ben Whole Grain Brown Rice. Sodium is essential to humans, used for regulating blood pressure and blood volume, and critical for muscle and nerve function.

Excess dietary sodium can lead to hypertension, and may have more serious implications in people with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis or renal disease. Sodium occurs naturally in most foods but most dietary sodium is added, particularly to processed foods. By some estimates, as much as 75% of dietary sodium comes from processed foods (United States Department of Health and Human Services, HHS, 2005), and purchased meals may also be high in sodium. The Recommended Daily Intake for sodium is 2300 mg/day for healthy adults and 1500 mg/day for persons with hypertension and other health considerations. Salt is always added to the local dish rice and peas during the cooking process (Samuda et al., 1998a,b) and many households also add salt and sometimes

butter or margarine to plain rice during or after cooking. The sodium content of such a widely consumed staple as rice becomes of utmost importance.

Even at the upper end of the range, the sodium content of rice is relatively low and without addition

The potassium content of white rice samples was found to range from 465 to 1659 mg/kg while the range for brown rice samples was 833-3097 mg/kg. The average for white rice content is somewhat lower than that quoted in other publications while the mean for brown rice was similar (Mohammed and Spyrou, 2009; Phuong et al., 1999). Roland Black Japonica rice had the highest concentration of potassium while the lowest concentration was found in Mahatma Jasmine rice. Potassium is the third most abundant mineral in the human body and is essential to human life.

Most of the iron in the body is found in heme proteins such as hemoglobin and myoglobin, both involved in oxygen transport. Iron is also found as a constituent of heme enzymes such as cytochromes, catalases and peroxidizes and other non heme compounds (McDowell, 1992). The amount of bioavailable iron in rice and other staple plants is low, and the phytic acid present in rice may add to this lack of bioavailability (Glahn et al., 2002). This is a likely contributor to the global iron deficiency problem. The polishing of rice may remove phytic acid and polyphenols, and enrichment may be an important tool in combating iron deficiency (Liang, 2007).

The iron content of white rice ranged from < 3.10 to 153 mg/kg while the range for brown rice samples was 12.8-38.2 mg/kg. The mean value found in white rice was 22.3 mg/kg and the mean in brown rice was 20.1 mg/kg. 44% of the white rice samples had iron levels below the limit of detection, and the reported mean is likely a reflection of enrichment. The highest value was found in Riceland Enriched White Rice.

The second highest concentration was Mahatma Long Grain Enriched rice. The bulk rice most consumed by Jamaicans had the lowest detected concentration. The WHO

## 3.2.6. Magnesium

Magnesium concentrations in white rice ranged from 176 to 562 mg/kg, and 340 to 1450 mg/kg in brown rice.

The mean concentration found in white rice was 371 mg/kg and the mean in brown rice was 1205 mg/kg. Bulk rice had a value of 381 mg/kg and as such may not be an adequate source of dietary magnesium, but several types of Jamaican foods do contain significant levels of magnesium (Howe et al., 2005). Magnesium toxicity whether by dietary intake or parenteral administration is improbable as excessive magnesium is excreted (Rude, 1998). Magnesium

deficiency in animals and humans however, is well known and described in literature. Symptoms range from growth retardation, nausea, muscle weakness, tetany and this deficiency may affect cardiac function (McDowell, 1992). It was thought the typical westernized diet provided adequate magnesium; however a significant amount of the US population may be falling short of recommended intake amounts (Rude, 1998). This may suggest that a tendency toward deficiency is more likely than previously estimated. According to the NIH, a cup of cooked brown rice contains approximately 80 mg of magnesium, which would be about 20% of RDA.

## 3.2.7. Manganese

The manganese concentrations in white rice samples ranged from 5.02 to 17.1 mg/kg; the range for brown rice was 5.1943.5 mg/kg. The mean concentration of manganese in the white rice samples analyzed was 10.5 mg/kg and 26.5 mg/kg in brown rice samples, with Roland Black Japonica rice having the highest levels. Brown rice is known as a good source of manganese and several of the samples had manganese levels in excess of 30 mg/ kg. Manganese is essential to human beings. It can function as an enzyme activator for several enzymes and as a component of some metalloenzymes.

It is also important for bone growth, carbohydrate and lipid metabolism. Because of its ubiquity in foods, deficiency is unlikely in an adequate diet.

Many of the elements detected in the rice samples such as some rare earth elements (cerium, europium, lanthanum and samarium), scandium and antimony appear to have no definitive physiological function in the human body. Some, such as scandium are considered non-toxic while others like antimony and some of its compounds can be toxic.

It is possible however that emerging research may change the known essentiality of these trace elements.

## 3.3.1. Bromine

The bromine content of the rice samples varied greatly, from 0.273 to 113 mg/kg in white rice and 0.467 to 19.97 mg/kg in brown rice.

The mean concentration was 10.7 mg/kg in white rice and 3.39 mg/kg in brown rice. The sample containing 113 mg/kg was Kendel Jasmine Rice; most of the samples contain less than 1 mg/kg bromine, making this value remarkable. The second highest sample contained 29.2 mg/kg and is also jasmine rice; however no inferences may be drawn based on variety or origin.

## 3.3.2. Rubidium

The range of rubidium in white rice was 0.70-9.10 mg/kg with a mean of 4.75 mg/kg; for brown rice the range was 2.13-16.4 mg/kg with a mean of 7.6 mg/kg. The Jamaican field trial composite sample was 2.92 mg/kg.

The essentiality of rubidium has not been determined although evidence suggests a number of roles in various human systems. As an alkali metal rubidium has the same oxidative state as potassium and has been suggested, is exchangeable with potassium in biological systems because of this chemical similarity. Interest in rubidium's role as an element with antidepressant properties has come to the fore with the discovery of deficiencies in uremic patients undergoing dialysis (Canavese et al., 2008; Nielsen, 2003). Although deficiency or excess states in humans have yet to be described, a tentative requirement of 400 m g/day has been suggested. Cereals are not considered to be significant sources of rubidium but the ubiquity of the element in foodstuffs, especially raw fruits, vegetables and meat make deficiency unlikely (Anke et al., 2005). The rubidium found in the rice samples analyzed suggests that the contribution would be significant from this source. More research is necessary to determine the biological role of this element.

## 3.3.3. Strontium

Strontium ranged from 1.48 to 2.73 mg/kg and 2.01 to 4.19 mg/ kg in white rice and brown rice samples respectively.

Strontium is an alkali earth metal with chemical similarity to calcium. Because of this it can exchange with calcium in bone (IPCS, 2010). Studies suggest that strontium has bone density increasing properties (Neuprez and Reginster, 2008) but at higher concentrations this element appears to impair normal bone development (Verberckmoes et al., 2003). Strontium has no clearly established biological role and no daily intake has been established as a deficiency state has yet to be identified. Strontium is also generally regarded as non toxic (Bonjour et al., 2009).

## 3.3.4. Vanadium

The range of vanadium concentrations in white rice was < 0.017-0.072 mg/kg; for brown rice the range was < 0.0210.091 mg/kg. Vanadium was detected in approximated 73% of the samples analyzed with a mean value of 0.037 mg/kg in white rice and 0.057 mg/kg in brown rice.

The highest overall value of 0.091 mg/kg was found in the Kendel Brown Gold Basmati Rice. Studies have suggested that vanadium has a role in the regulation of several enzymes and also as a cofactor in hormone, lipid and glucose metabolism as well as the building of bones and teeth. However the essentiality of vanadium has as yet not been established. Vanadium compounds are regarded as toxic but the generally low concentrations of vanadium found in the foods and the low absorption of vanadium in the gastrointestinal tract means that toxicity from the ingestion of uncontaminated food is unlikely.

## 3.2.8. Molybdenum

The range of molybdenum values found in white rice samples was 0.438-1.62 mg/kg and the range for brown rice samples was 0.447-1.20 mg/kg. The mean values for white rice and brown rice were 0.790 and 0.770 mg/kg respectively. The highest value was found in the Mahatma long grain enriched rice. The bulk rice most consumed by Jamaicans had a value of 0.48 mg/kg. Molybdenum is an essential trace nutrient.

In humans it plays an important role in the regulation of calcium, magnesium and copper metabolism. It is biologically active as a co factor to several enzymes as well as the oxidation of sulfite and the formation of uric acid (McDowell, 1992). Because of the relatively low daily requirements of this nutrient (RDA, 45 m g/day for adults) and high tolerance (up to 10 mg/day) deficiency and toxicity from balanced dietary intake is unlikely.

## 3.2.9. Phosphorus

Phosphorus in the white rice samples ranged from 335 to 2591 mg/kg, and from 931 to 4339 mg/kg in brown rice.

The mean total phosphorus in the white rice samples analyzed was 1203 mg/ kg; the mean in the brown rice samples was 3361 mg/kg. Not surprisingly the highest result overall was obtained in a sample of brown rice. Also of note is the black japonica variety, which was found to contain 4137 mg/kg of phosphorus. Several brands of brown rice were found to have levels closer to the maximum value observed in this study.

Phosphorus, as phosphates, is among the most abundant of mineral elements in the human body. Deficiencies in phosphorus nutrition have historically been seen in rickets and osteomalacia (which may also be caused by an inadequacy in calcium and/or vitamin D) as well as other bone symptoms and skeletal deformities. It does not appear that the typical adult diet is deficient in phosphorus. Of great importance is the presence of phosphorus in its storage form phytic acid. Phytic acid is considered an anti-nutrient because of its binding affinity for several elements of nutritional consequence such as iron, zinc and calcium. About 80% of phosphorus in rice is stored as phytic acid (Mohammed, 2008). About 50% of the mineral content is retained in the bran. This is removed when polishing rice. It is for this reason that brown rice would have more phosphorus and consequently more phytic acid. In cases where rice is an important source of calories the already low mineral content may be further reduced by the relatively high levels of phytic acid.

## 3.2.10. Potassium

The potassium content of white rice samples was found to range from 465 to 1659 mg/kg while the range for brown rice samples was 833-3097 mg/kg. The mean for white rice was 913 mg/kg and 2157 mg/kg for brown rice. The average for white rice content is somewhat lower than that quoted in other publications while the mean for brown rice was similar (Mohammed and Spyrou, 2009; Phuong et al., 1999). Roland Black Japonica rice had the highest concentration of potassium while the lowest concentration was found in Mahatma Jasmine rice. Potassium is the third most abundant mineral in the human body and is essential to human life.

## 3.2.11. Selenium

Selenium values for white rice ranged from < 0.028 to 0.236 mg/ kg and those for brown rice from < 0.058 to 0.204 mg/kg. Seventysix percent of the samples had detectable levels of selenium with a mean value of 0.108 mg/kg in white rice and 0.131 mg/kg in brown rice.

It has been shown that staples grown in soils with high Se bioavailability will have relatively high selenium content, with the converse being the case in soils with low selenium content (IPCS, 1987). The ability of selenium to bind toxic heavy metals, especially mercury, mitigates its various pathological effects, especially those related to the brain of the developing fetus, has been known for some time if not always highlighted in studies on risk of mercury exposure (Berry, 2008).

## 3.2.12. Sodium

The sodium content of the white rice samples had a range of 1.65-11.4 mg/kg while the brown rice samples ranged from 5.07 to 48.1 mg/kg. The mean concentration of sodium in the white rice samples was 6.00 mg/kg; the mean for brown rice is 15.1 mg/kg. The highest sodium was found in Uncle Ben Whole Grain Brown Rice. Sodium is essential to humans, used for regulating blood pressure and blood volume, and critical for muscle and nerve function.

Excess dietary sodium can lead to hypertension, and may have more serious implications in people with congestive heart failure, cirrhosis or renal disease. Sodium occurs naturally in most foods but most dietary sodium is added, particularly to processed foods. By some estimates, as much as 75% of dietary sodium comes from processed foods (United States Department of Health and Human Services, HHS, 2005), and purchased meals may also be high in sodium. The Recommended Daily Intake for sodium is 2300 mg/day for healthy adults and 1500 mg/day for persons with hypertension and other health considerations. Salt is always added to the local dish rice and peas during the cooking process (Samuda et al., 1998a,b) and many households also add salt and sometimes

butter or margarine to plain rice during or after cooking. The sodium content of such a widely consumed staple as rice becomes of utmost importance.

Even at the upper end of the range, the sodium content of rice is relatively low and without addition of salt would not contribute significantly to dietary sodium intake.

## 3.2.13. Sulfur

The range of sulfur values for white rice was 912-1328 mg/kg, while for brown rice it was 1118-1671 mg/kg. The mean concentration of sulfur found in white rice was 1131 mg/kg. The mean in brown rice was 1291 mg/kg. Sulfur is a minor constituent of fats, body fluids, and skeletal minerals and is essential to life.

It is a component of many proteins due to its presence in the amino acids methionine and cysteine and is present in biotin and thiamine. Hemoglobin also contains sulfur (McDowell, 1992). Dietary intake guidelines have not been established for sulfur but it is generally accepted that a diet sufficient in protein provides sufficient sulfur, about 850 mg/day.

## 3.3.4. Vanadium

The range of vanadium concentrations in white rice was < 0.017-0.072 mg/kg; for brown rice the range was < 0.0210.091 mg/kg. Vanadium was detected in approximated 73% of the samples analyzed with a mean value of 0.037 mg/kg in white rice and 0.057 mg/kg in brown rice.

The highest overall value of 0.091 mg/kg was found in the Kendel Brown Gold Basmati Rice. Studies have suggested that vanadium has a role in the regulation of several enzymes and also as a cofactor in hormone, lipid and glucose metabolism as well as the building of bones and teeth. However the essentiality of vanadium has as yet not been established. Vanadium compounds are regarded as toxic but the generally low concentrations of vanadium found in the foods and the low absorption of vanadium in the gastrointestinal tract means that toxicity from the ingestion of uncontaminated food is unlikely.

## 3.5. Rice from local field trial

Jamaica's Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries has undertaken field trials of rice over the past few years.

As recently as January 2009, there were nine varieties of rice being compared for yield, time to maturity and nutritive value. The test sample analyzed for this work represented a composite sample of Prosequisa 4, a Dominican variety, being tested at the Amity Hall farms in the parish of St. Catherine.

The levels of many of the elements in the rice from the local field trial are not remarkable, either in that they would not contribute significantly to dietary intake, or they do not deviate much from the mean values obtained for all samples. Of note however are Ag, Cu and Se; of all the samples analyzed, the Jamaican-grown rice contains the highest levels of these elements. The local rice also contains the second highest levels of Co, Mo and Zn. The lowest levels of As and Br were also detected in this sample. While the high level of Zn found in the local rice cannot at this time be related to the high blood levels found in Jamaica (as it is not yet commercially available), it may be related to the considerable levels of Zn in Jamaican soils, which have a mean Zn content of 205 mg/kg (Lalor, 1996).

## 4. Conclusions

While rice is considered to be one of the major staples consumed in Jamaica, the actual contribution to elemental nutrition may not be significant; especially considering that the most widely consumed variety is white bulk rice which is not enriched.

It is noteworthy that the brown rice analyzed contains, on average, significantly greater concentrations of, Cr, Cu, K, Mg, Mn, Na, P, and Zn in comparison with the white rice samples. It is also of note that the mean Ca and Fe values are lower for brown rice than for white, and is likely due to the number of white rice samples which are enriched and/or parboiled.

Average per capita consumption of rice by Jamaicans is estimated at 71.2 g/day (FAOSTAT, 2007).

This is far less than in major rice consuming countries (Kennedy et al., 2002) such as Vietnam (464.7 g/day), Laos (470.0 g/day) and Myanmar (577.9 g/ day). Rice in the Jamaican diet is said to contribute 11.0% of dietary energy, 9.2% of protein and 1.5% of fat. Additionally, unlike in high consuming countries (particularly those in Asia), rice is not eaten at every meal and indeed may only be eaten at one meal per day, as ground provisions and other cereals or cereal products are also commonly consumed, and meats and vegetables likely play a more significant role in the Jamaican diet than in those of other major rice consuming nations. Notwithstanding, the pending shift toward rice cultivation in Jamaica warrants further study of the elemental content of the locally grown product, not only from a nutritive standpoint, but also because of the natural enrichment of heavy metals in some Jamaican soils. If rice production is to commence on a scale large enough to impact Jamaica's reliance on the importation of this staple this is among the criteria that should be used to select appropriate soils for cultivation.

Rice provides between 14 and 17% of the RDI for selenium. Selenium forms complexes with cadmium and mercury (McDowell, 1992) and with the potential for the Jamaican population to be exposed to both cadmium and mercury, selenium in the diet may take on added significance.

No RDI has been established for sulfur, but an adequate intake of 850 mg/day has been suggested.

Although no more than 11% of this would come from rice, a diet with sufficient protein should provide adequate sulfur. Organic sulfur compounds have a low degree of toxicity (Parcell, 2002) and since protein is the major source of sulfur a deficiency of this element is likely a protein deficiency.

The daily intake of aluminum from rice is estimated to be highest from bulk rice, with 16.7% of the PTWI for males and 17.9% of the PTWI for females. The estimated contribution from arsenic is highest from the mean concentration for white rice, and is 9.5% of the PTWI for males and 10.2% of the PTWI for females. The greatest contribution from cadmium is 8.4% of the PTWI for males and 9.0% for females, estimated from mean brown rice concentration. The highest estimate for mercury intake is obtained from brown rice, at 11.1% of the PTWI for males and 12.0% for females.

Although none of these numbers exceed the PTWI it is noteworthy that these estimates are only for rice consumption.

Contributions to the PTWI of these toxic elements from other food sources and drinking water will need to be considered to give a more robust picture of dietary exposure. The contribution of aluminum from bulk rice is of particular concern as it is the most widely consumed brand of rice in Jamaica. It can be argued that the PTWI estimates for Cd and Hg represent what is likely the maximum exposure based on the detection limits of the technique applied and that the actual intake of these elements may be lower.

## 3.5. Rice from local field trial

Jamaica's Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries has undertaken field trials of rice over the past few years.

As recently as January 2009, there were nine varieties of rice being compared for yield, time to maturity and nutritive value. The test sample analyzed for this work represented a composite sample of Prosequisa 4, a Dominican variety, being tested at the Amity Hall farms in the parish of St. Catherine.

The levels of many of the elements in the rice from the local field trial are not remarkable, either in that they would not contribute significantly to dietary intake, or they do not deviate much from the mean values obtained for all samples. Of note however are Ag, Cu and Se; of all the samples analyzed, the Jamaican-grown rice contains the highest levels of these elements. The local rice also contains the second highest levels of Co, Mo and Zn. The lowest levels of As and Br were also detected in this sample. While the high level of Zn found in the local rice cannot at this time be related to the high blood levels found in Jamaica (as it is not yet commercially available), it may be related to the considerable levels of Zn in Jamaican soils, which have a mean Zn content of 205 mg/kg (Lalor, 1996).

For many elements, including S, Ca, P, Zn, Cu, Na and Se, the content of the Jamaican rice was higher than that of white rice samples collected, and higher than the mean value found in brown rice samples in this survey. The experimental Jamaican brown rice had 3705 mg/kg of phosphorus. Although when polishing occurs it can be expected that this number will be reduced significantly it may be prudent to consider phosphorus in prospective growing soils and the impact of phytic acid on mineral nutrition when selecting growing areas.

For several elements, including Br, As, Cr, Mo, Fe, Mn and Cd, the content of the Jamaican rice sample was markedly lower than the mean values found in both white and brown rice. The most profound discrepancy is seen in the Br value for white rice. Fe in the Jamaican rice sample may be lower due to enrichment of the commercial rice samples.

The lower values for As and Cd are encouraging given that some Jamaican soils are known to have naturally elevated levels of these elements (Lalor, 1996), but until further sampling from field trials can be done, no definite conclusions can be drawn.

## 4. Conclusions

While rice is considered to be one of the major staples consumed in Jamaica, the actual contribution to elemental nutrition may not be significant; especially considering that the most widely consumed variety is white bulk rice which is not enriched.

It is noteworthy that the brown rice analyzed contains, on average, significantly greater concentrations of, Cr, Cu, K, Mg, Mn, Na, P, and Zn in comparison with the white rice samples. It is also of note that the mean Ca and Fe values are lower for brown rice than for white, and is likely due to the number of white rice samples which are enriched and/or parboiled.

Average per capita consumption of rice by Jamaicans is estimated at 71.2 g/day (FAOSTAT, 2007).

This is far less than in major rice consuming countries (Kennedy et al., 2002) such as Vietnam (464.7 g/day), Laos (470.0 g/day) and Myanmar (577.9 g/ day). Rice in the Jamaican diet is said to contribute 11.0% of dietary energy, 9.2% of protein and 1.5% of fat. Additionally, unlike in high consuming countries (particularly those in Asia), rice is not eaten at every meal and indeed may only be eaten at one meal per day, as ground provisions and other cereals or cereal products are also commonly consumed, and meats and vegetables likely play a more significant role in the Jamaican diet than in

It is noteworthy that the brown rice analyzed contains, on average, significantly greater concentrations of, Cr, Cu, K, Mg, Mn, Na, P, and Zn in comparison with the white rice samples. It is also of note that the mean Ca and Fe values are lower for brown rice than for white, and is likely due to the number of white rice samples which are enriched and/or parboiled.

Bulk rice provides on average 6% and 8% of the RDI for magnesium for males and females respectively, the same as white rice. Brown rice contributes 20% and 27% and this is in line with NIH estimates of a cup of brown rice providing approximately 20% of the RDI.

Brown rice is a significant source of copper with the average intake accounting for 23% of the RDI. The same holds true for molybdenum, with brown rice providing as much as 122% of the RDI. Copper is found in a variety of foods and its relatively low RDI means that deficiency, although reported, is rare. Deficiency may be as a result of interfering factors affecting bioavailability such as iron deficiency, molybdenum and excessive zinc ingestion (Kumar, 2007). Unpublished data generated at ICENS, showed relatively high blood levels of zinc and this was shown to have implications on the copper status. The symptoms of molybdenum toxicity are generally those of copper deficiency (McDowell, 1992) and so the effect of zinc on copper may require further investigation.

There is potentially a significant contribution to phosphorus intake from rice, with an estimated contribution of 12% of the RDI from white rice and 34% from brown rice. A significant portion of this phosphorus is as the anti-nutrient phytic acid and this has implications for the bioavailability of zinc, iron and manganese.

Rice appears to be a significant source of manganese for the Jamaican population with white rice contributing to 32% and 41% of the Adequate Intake (AI) for males and females respectively; bulk rice contributes 16 and 20% but of note is brown rice which on average supplies 82% of the male AI and 105% of the female AI. Although the upper limit established is 11 mg/day for adults it bears noting that the Jamaican diet has other significant sources of manganese including legumes and leafy vegetables (Howe et al., 2005) and although toxicity by dietary means is still unlikely, deficiency does not appear to be an issue.

The contribution to dietary sodium intake is insignificant, which may be advantageous given the propensity for excess sodium in the modern diet. Jamaica has a point prevalence of hypertension of 30.8% in the 15-and-over age group (Ragoobirsingh et al., 2002) and potassium is known to have an effect on the development and management of hypertension (Sica, 2008). It is therefore noteworthy that rice is not a rich source of potassium with brown rice contributing the most to the RDI at 3.3%.

Zinc and iron deficiencies have been well described in literature and the WHO lists these as leading causes of illness and disease in low income countries. Rice provides between 10 and 18% of the RDI for zinc however, unpublished data generated at ICENS, showed zinc levels in a survey of Jamaican blood to be among the highest in the world for men and women; about 42% above a world mean

presented in a literature review. While this warrants further investigation this may suggest that zinc deficiency is not a concern in the Jamaican diet. The RDI for iron is significantly different for males and females, thus, while males may obtain as much as 20% of their RDI from rice (using average white rice data) the contribution to RDI for females is, at best, only 9%. The relatively high levels of iron in white rice suggested by the mean are likely the result of enrichment and/or parboiling which puts the iron content on par with brown rice values.

Although cereals such as rice are generally considered low in iron the values for both brown and white rice are similar to the iron content of locally grown Jamaican foods. Jamaican fruits, legumes, leafy vegetables, root vegetables and other root crops had mean iron levels of 6.7, 30.0, 15.5, 12.9 and 9.6 mg/kg respectively (Howe et al., 2005).

Rice provides between 14 and 17% of the RDI for selenium. Selenium forms complexes with cadmium and mercury (McDowell, 1992) and with the potential for the Jamaican population to be exposed to both cadmium and mercury, selenium in the diet may take on added significance.

No RDI has been established for sulfur, but an adequate intake of 850 mg/day has been suggested.

The daily intake of aluminum from rice is estimated to be highest from bulk rice, with 16.7% of the PTWI for males and 17.9% of the PTWI for females. The estimated contribution from arsenic is highest from the mean concentration for white rice, and is 9.5% of the PTWI for males and 10.2% of the PTWI for females. The greatest contribution from cadmium is 8.4% of the PTWI for males and 9.0% for females, estimated from mean brown rice concentration. The highest estimate for mercury intake is obtained from brown rice, at 11.1% of the PTWI for males and 12.0% for females.

Although none of these numbers exceed the PTWI it is noteworthy that these estimates are only for rice consumption.

Contributions to the PTWI of these toxic elements from other food sources and drinking water will need to be considered to give a more robust picture of dietary exposure. The contribution of aluminum from bulk rice is of particular concern as it is the most widely consumed brand of rice in Jamaica. It can be argued that the PTWI estimates for Cd and Hg represent what is likely the maximum exposure based on the detection limits of the technique applied and that the actual intake of these elements may be lower.

## 3.5. Rice from local field trial

Jamaica's Ministry of Agriculture and Fisheries has undertaken field trials of rice over the past few years.

As recently as January 2009, there were nine varieties of rice being compared for yield, time to maturity and nutritive value. The test sample analyzed for this work represented a composite sample of Prosequisa 4, a Dominican variety, being tested at the Amity Hall farms in the parish of St. Catherine.

The levels of many of the elements in the rice from the local field trial are not remarkable, either in that they would not contribute significantly to dietary intake, or they do not deviate much from the mean values obtained for all samples. Of note however are Ag, Cu and Se; of all the samples analyzed, the Jamaican-grown rice contains the highest levels of these elements. The local rice also contains the second highest levels of Co, Mo and Zn. The lowest levels of As and Br were also detected in this sample. While the high level of Zn found in the local rice cannot at this time be related to the high blood levels found in Jamaica (as it is not yet commercially available), it may be related to the considerable levels of Zn in Jamaican soils, which have a mean Zn content of 205 mg/kg (Lalor, 1996).

For many elements, including S, Ca, P, Zn, Cu, Na and Se, the content of the Jamaican rice was higher than that of white rice samples collected, and higher than the mean value found in brown rice samples in this survey. The experimental Jamaican brown rice had 3705 mg/kg of phosphorus. Although when polishing occurs it can be expected that this number will be reduced significantly it may be prudent to consider phosphorus in prospective growing soils and the impact of phytic acid on mineral nutrition when selecting growing areas.

For several elements, including Br, As, Cr, Mo, Fe, Mn and Cd, the content of the Jamaican rice sample was markedly lower than the mean values found in both white and brown rice. The most profound discrepancy is seen in the Br value for white rice. Fe in the Jamaican rice sample may be lower due to enrichment of the commercial rice samples.

The lower values for As and Cd are encouraging given that some Jamaican soils are known to have naturally elevated levels of these elements (Lalor, 1996), but until further sampling from field trials can be done, no definite conclusions can be drawn.

## 4. Conclusions

While rice is considered to be one of the major staples consumed in Jamaica, the actual contribution to elemental nutrition may not be significant; especially considering that the most widely consumed variety is white bulk rice which is not enriched.

It is noteworthy that the brown rice analyzed contains, on average, significantly greater concentrations of, Cr, Cu, K, Mg, Mn, Na, P, and Zn in comparison with the white rice samples. It is also of note that the mean Ca and Fe values are lower for brown rice than for white, and is likely due to the number of white rice samples which are enriched and/or parboiled.

Average per capita consumption of rice by Jamaicans is estimated at 71.2 g/day (FAOSTAT, 2007).

This is far less than in major rice consuming countries (Kennedy et al., 2002) such as Vietnam (464.7 g/day), Laos (470.0 g/day) and Myanmar (577.9 g/ day). Rice in the Jamaican diet is said to contribute 11.0% of dietary energy, 9.2% of protein and 1.5% of fat. Additionally, unlike in high consuming countries (particularly those in Asia), rice is not eaten at every meal and indeed may only be eaten at one meal per day, as ground provisions and other cereals or cereal products are also commonly consumed, and meats and vegetables likely play a more significant role in the Jamaican diet than in those of other major rice consuming nations. Notwithstanding, the pending shift toward rice cultivation in Jamaica warrants further study of the elemental content of the locally grown product, not only from a nutritive standpoint, but also because of the natural enrichment of heavy metals in some Jamaican soils. If rice production is to commence on a scale large enough to impact Jamaica's reliance on the importation of this staple this is among the criteria that should be used to select appropriate soils for cultivation.

Methylmercury was more ef /uniFB01 ciently translocated to the endosperm than inorganic mercury.

Concentrations of HgT and other trace elements were signi /uniFB01 cantly higher in unmilled brown rice ( p < 0.05), while MeHg content was similar ( p > 0.20), indicating MeHg in /uniFB01 ltrated the endosperm (i.e., white rice) more ef /uniFB01 ciently than inorganic Hg(II).

## 3.2. HgT and MeHg concentrations in rice plants

HgT and MeHg concentrations for rice plants harvested in July and September are shown in Figs. 2 and 3.

In both months, mean leaf HgT levels were similar or higher than root HgT levels, which suggested stems were not the only source of HgT to the leaves. Findings were consistent with previous research that demonstrated leaf HgT was mainly accumulated from the atmosphere and not the roots (Ericksen et al., 2003; Rea et al., 2002; Stamenkovic and Gustin, 2009; Zhang et al., 2010d).

In July leaf HgT levels were signi /uniFB01 cantly higher in site 1 compared to sites 2 and 3 (ANOVA, p < 0.05, n ¼ 6) (site 1: 300 /C6 47 ng/g, site 2: 42 /C6 12 ng/g, site 3: 52 /C6 24 ng/g). Site 1 was located downwind from a cooking oil factory emitting pollution from a smokestack at the same time rice plants were collected, although atmospheric Hg was not measured. Site 2 was located upwind from the factory and Site 3 was further downwind (Fig. 1). The mean HgT value for leaves at site 1 (300 ng/g) was derived from rice plants collected in 2 paddies (leaf HgT paddy 1: 270 /C6 14 ng/g, n ¼ 2 replicates; leaf HgT paddy 2: 330 /C6 90 ng/g, n ¼ 4 replicates). In contrast to July, leaf HgT levels in September were similar at all 3 sites (one-way ANOVA, p > 0.05, n ¼ 6), which suggested HgT was not stored between July and September in the leaves. Instead, inorganic Hg(II) was possibly reemitted to the atmosphere from the leaves (Graydon et al., 2006; Stamenkovic and Gustin, 2009), or transported to other plant components, or exuded from the roots to the soil (Marschner, 1995).

Samples from all three sites were collected on July 30 e 31, 2009, when rice plants were in the mid-reproductive stage (i.e., booting, when the hull was formed but not yet /uniFB01 lled), and on September 5, 2009, when paddy /uniFB01 elds were dried and mature rice grain was within 10 days of harvest. Within each site, two neighboring paddies were sampled in July and September. In site 3, a different pair of paddies was sampled in September, since rice grain from paddies sampled in July was already harvested. In each paddy /uniFB01 eld, the study area was limited to approximately 15 /C2 8 m, although each paddy was several times larger (e.g., site 1: 85 /C2 8 m; site 2: 38 /C2 15 m, site 3: 30 /C2 90 m). In July and September, two individual plants were collected and composited from each rice paddy ( n ¼ 6 paddies) for analysis of rootsoil, root, stem, leaf, and rice grain.

In July, one composite soil sample was collected from 4 points within the study area of each rice paddy, and in September, one composite sample of rice grain was harvested from 10 plants within each study area. Spatial variability for HgT and MeHg is likely within the rice paddy; therefore, composite samples were collected (for soil in July, and for rice grain in September) to compare with root-soil and rice grain from individual plants, collected in July and September, respectively. In September, a surface water sample (used for irrigation) was collected within each site near the paddies, and in the canal downstream from the cooking oil factory between sites 1 and 2 (Fig. 1).

In September 2009, one rice sample was collected near Wanshan, in eastern Guizhou province, China, where traditional /uniFB02 ooded irrigation methods were practiced (Fig. 1).

## 2.2. Laboratory methods

## 2.2.3. Hg species

HgT was measured in aqueous samples following the addition of 0.5% (v/v) 0.2 N bromine monochloride, reduction with hydroxylamine hydrochloride, further reduction with tin chloride, purging of volatile Hg o onto gold traps, and detection of Hg o by cold vapor atomic /uniFB02 uorescence spectrophotometry (CVAFS, Brooks Rand Model III, Seattle, USA), using methods detailed in EPA Method 1631, Revision E (USEPA, 2002).

MeHginaqueous samples was analyzed following distillation, adjustment of pH using 2 M acetate buffer, ethylation with 1% sodium tetraethylborate, capture of gaseous methylethylmercury onto Tenax traps, thermal desorption from traps, separation by gas chromatography, and detection by CVAFS (Brooks Rand Model III, Seattle, USA), as described in EPA Method 1630 (USEPA, 2001a).

Solid-phase HgT concentrations in rice and soil samples were analyzed with a portable Hg vapor analyzer (Lumex, Model RA-915 þ /PYRO-915 þ , St. Petersburg, Russia), using methods described in EPA Method 7473 (USEPA,1998). No pre-digestion

steps were necessary. MeHg concentrations in soil (1 e 2 g) and rice samples ( w 1 g) were analyzed using solvent extraction with dichloromethane (CH2Cl2). Soil samples were leached in 1.5 mL 2 M copper sulfate, 7.5 mL 25% HNO3 and 10 mL CH2Cl2 (Liang et al., 2004). For rice samples, 5 mL of 25% KOH e water were added and samples were heated for 3 h at 75 /C14 C in a water bath, then 5 mL concentrated HCl and 10 mL CH2Cl2 were added (based on Liang et al., 1996). After leaching, rice and soil samples were vigorously shaken ( w 1 h), centrifuged (25 min, 3500 RPM, 25 /C14 C), the phases were separated by suction leaving the organic phase, about 30 mL Milli-Q-H2O were added, and samples were heated in a 50 /C14 Cwaterbath for 1.5 h to evacuate CH2Cl2. MeHg was detected using CVAFS, as described for aqueous MeHg in distilled samples.

Concentrations for all solid-phase samples are reported in dry weight.

## 2.2.4. Organic content

HgT and MeHg concentrations for wet soil samples were converted to dry weight following oven drying to constant weight at 60 /C14 C. Organic carbon content was determined for dried samples by percent loss on ignition (LOI) at 550 /C14 Cfor two hours.

## 2.2.5. Other elements

Mg, K, Mn, Zn, Cu, and Ni were determined in brown and white rice grains following EPA Method 3050b (USEPA,1996).

All elements were analyzed using /uniFB02 ame atomic absorption spectrometry (AAS, Model 5100 PC, Perkin Elmer, Inc., Waltham, USA), aside from Ni, which was analyzed by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry (GV Instruments, Cheshire, UK).

## 2.2.6. QA/QC

HgT, MeHgand other trace elements were quanti /uniFB01 edusingdaily calibration curves with the coef /uniFB01 cient of variation ( r 2 ) > 0.99. The minimum detection levels (MDLs) for HgT and MeHg were estimated from the region of the standard curve where there was a signi /uniFB01 cant change in sensitivity (40 CFR, Appendix B to Part 136, De /uniFB01 nition and Procedure for Determination of the Method Detection Limit).

MDLs for trace elements (Mg, K, Mn, Zn, Cu, and Ni) were based on instrument aqueous detection levels, corrected for the total volume (50 mL) and the mass of rice digested (1 g). MDLs, percent recovery of matrix spikes and standard reference material, and relative percent difference between replicate analyses (RPDs) are summarized in Table 1.

## 2.2.2. Rice milling

Air-dried mature rice grain from Hubei province was milled at the Research Center for Eco-Environmental Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) (Beijing, China), and air-dried mature rice samples from Wanshan, Guizhou province, were milled at the Institute of Geochemistry, CAS (Guiyang, China), following methods described by Sun et al.

(2008) and using the same instruments at both locations. Brie /uniFB02 y, the hull was removed exposing the edible rice (i.e., the caryopsis, referred to as unpolished brown rice) (Huller, JLGJ4.5, China); for half the sample, the bran was removed to produce polished white rice (Rice mill, JNMJ3, China); lastly, both brown and white rice samples were ground to a powder in a blender that was cleaned with ethanol after each sample to avoid cross-contamination. Approximately 7% of the bran was removed, which was slightly higher than the proportion of bran in commercial brown rice (6.3%, from Franz and Sampson, 2006).

## 2.2.3. Hg species

HgT was measured in aqueous samples following the addition of 0.5% (v/v) 0.2 N bromine monochloride, reduction with hydroxylamine hydrochloride, further reduction with tin chloride, purging of volatile Hg o onto gold traps, and detection of Hg o by cold vapor atomic /uniFB02 uorescence spectrophotometry (CVAFS, Brooks Rand Model III, Seattle, USA), using methods detailed in EPA Method 1631, Revision E (USEPA, 2002).

MeHginaqueous samples was analyzed following distillation, adjustment of pH using 2 M acetate buffer, ethylation with 1% sodium tetraethylborate, capture of gaseous methylethylmercury onto Tenax traps, thermal desorption from traps, separation by gas chromatography, and detection by CVAFS (Brooks Rand Model III, Seattle, USA), as described in EPA Method 1630 (USEPA, 2001a).

Solid-phase HgT concentrations in rice and soil samples were analyzed with a portable Hg vapor analyzer (Lumex, Model RA-915 þ /PYRO-915 þ , St. Petersburg, Russia), using methods described in EPA Method 7473 (USEPA,1998). No pre-digestion

steps were necessary. MeHg concentrations in soil (1 e 2 g) and rice samples ( w 1 g) were analyzed using solvent extraction with dichloromethane (CH2Cl2). Soil samples were leached in 1.5 mL 2 M copper sulfate, 7.5 mL 25% HNO3 and 10 mL CH2Cl2 (Liang et al., 2004). For rice samples, 5 mL of 25% KOH e water were added and samples were heated for 3 h at 75 /C14 C in a water bath, then 5 mL concentrated HCl and 10 mL CH2Cl2 were added (based on Liang et al., 1996). After leaching, rice and soil samples were vigorously shaken ( w 1 h), centrifuged (25 min, 3500 RPM, 25 /C14 C), the phases were separated by suction leaving the organic phase, about 30 mL Milli-Q-H2O were added, and samples were heated in a 50 /C14 Cwaterbath for 1.5 h to evacuate CH2Cl2. MeHg was detected using CVAFS, as described for aqueous MeHg in distilled samples.

Concentrations for all solid-phase samples are reported in dry weight.

## 2.2.4. Organic content

HgT and MeHg concentrations for wet soil samples were converted to dry weight following oven drying to constant weight at 60 /C14 C. Organic carbon content was determined for dried samples by percent loss on ignition (LOI) at 550 /C14 Cfor two hours.

## 2.2. Laboratory methods

## 2.2.1. Sample preparation and preservation

In July, rice samples (roots, stems, leaves, and seeds) were rinsed with Milli-Q H2O, air-dried for 2 weeks, then freeze-dried and ground for analysis.

In September, rinsed rice samples (roots, stems, and leaves) were air-dried for about 2 months and then ground for analysis. The stainless steel grinder was cleaned with ethanol after each sample to avoid cross-contamination. In September, aqueous samples were collected in 100 mL borosilicate bottles, which were acid-cleaned (20% HNO3) and rinsed with Milli-Q H2O, followed by heating in an oven at 550 /C14 C to thermally desorb Hg. Filtered (0.22 m M) and un /uniFB01 ltered aqueous samples were immediately acidi /uniFB01 ed to 0.5% HCl at Tuanlin Experimental Station, and stored in a dark refrigerator (4 /C14 C). Soil samples were collected in acid-cleaned plastic tubes and frozen at Tuanlin Experimental Station. All samples were transported back to the Institute of Geochemistry in Guiyang ( < 1 day of travel), where soil samples (for HgT and MeHg analysis) and 45 mL aliquots of aqueous samples (for MeHg analysis) were stored frozen until analysis ( /C0 20 /C14 C), while aqueous samples in borosilicate bottles (for HgT analysis) were refrigerated in the dark until analysis (4 /C14 C). All analyses were completed within 6 months following sample collection.

## 2.2.2. Rice milling

Air-dried mature rice grain from Hubei province was milled at the Research Center for Eco-Environmental Sciences, Chinese Academy of Sciences (CAS) (Beijing, China), and air-dried mature rice samples from Wanshan, Guizhou province, were milled at the Institute of Geochemistry, CAS (Guiyang, China), following methods described by Sun et al.

(2008) and using the same instruments at both locations. Brie /uniFB02 y, the hull was removed exposing the edible rice (i.e., the caryopsis, referred to as unpolished brown rice) (Huller, JLGJ4.5, China); for half the sample, the bran was removed to produce polished white rice (Rice mill, JNMJ3, China); lastly, both brown and white rice samples were ground to a powder in a blender that was cleaned with ethanol after each sample to avoid cross-contamination. Approximately 7% of the bran was removed, which was slightly higher than the proportion of bran in commercial brown rice (6.3%, from Franz and Sampson, 2006).

## 3.3. Calculation of daily MeHg ingestion rate

The average rice ingestion rate in 2008 in China was 270 g/d, which was based on the annual total rice consumption (130,778 /C2 10 3 t, from IRRI, 2010) and the population of China (1,324,655 /C2 10 3 , from PRB, 2010).

Using the mean MeHg levels in white rice (average: 1.2 ng/g, n ¼ 12), and assuming mean body weight is 60 kg, the mean daily MeHg intake rate from rice ingestion was 0.0054 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 , which was 17 times lower than the U.S. EPA recommended level (0.1 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 , USEPA, 2001b). Higher MeHg exposure levels were reported for brown rice in the Hg mining area in China, assuming the daily rice ingestion rate was 620 g/d (e.g., 0.26 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 from Qiu et al., 2008; 0.012 e 0.44 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 from Zhang et al., 2010c). Using the higher ingestion rate, the daily MeHg exposure level for this study was 0.012 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 (i.e., 8.1 times lower than the U.S. EPA reference dose, USEPA, 2001b), which indicated rice grain harvested from these paddies near Tuanlin village, Hubei province, China was not a signi /uniFB01 cant source of MeHg to humans.

Although this data set is small, results suggested at least a portion of HgT and MeHg in rice grain likely originated from the soil, which was consistent with observations by Meng et al. (2010). However, the slope for MeHg was twice as high as the slope for HgT (1.3 versus 0.64), which indicated MeHg was more ef /uniFB01 ciently translocated from the soil to the rice grain, or MeHg was not recycled in the plant once transferred to the rice grain. Additionally, uptake and translocation of Hg species from the soil into the grain may be independent of irrigation practices and soil Hg concentrations. AWD practices result in more aerobic rice paddies; however, drier conditions practiced in these AWD sites did not inhibit the uptake of Hg species from the soil and loading into the grain. This may re /uniFB02 ect the ' safe ' AWD approach, where paddies are intermittently /uniFB02 ooded, water savings are minimal (about 15%), and rice yield is not compromised (Bouman et al., 2007). There are other factors that may in /uniFB02 uence the uptake of HgT and MeHg, including soil pH (Overesch et al., 2007), interaction with other metals (Du et al., 2005) and/or sulfur species (Hu et al., 2007), and differences between cultivars (Liu et al., 2004), which were not examined in this analysis. More research is needed to calibrate the effect of AWD on uptake of nutrients and trace elements into the rice grain, to optimize nutritional quality and minimize exposure to toxic heavy metals.

## 3.5.

Hg speciation in brown and white rice

This is the /uniFB01 rst study, to the best of our knowledge, to report Hg species in both brown and white rice fractions. Earlier studies from Guizhou province reported MeHg levels in unpolished brown rice (e.g., Horvat et al., 2003; Meng et al., 2010; Qiu et al., 2006, 2008; Zhang et al., 2010a,d). Since milling may reduce micronutrient levels (Heinemann et al., 2005; Sellappan et al., 2009; Villareal et al., 1991), Hg species and other elements were compared between unpolished brown rice grain and polished white rice grain, and between sites (Table 2).

Using combined results from both composite and individual rice grain samples grown in 3 water-saving sites, HgT levels were signi /uniFB01 cantly higher in brown rice grain (paired t -test, p < 0.05,

n ¼ 12), while MeHg levels did not differ between the two fractions (paired t -test, p > 0.20, n ¼ 12) (Fig.

4). Concentrations of other trace elements (Mg, K, Mn, Zn, and Ni) were also signi /uniFB01 cantly higher in brown rice compared to white rice ( p < 0.05, n ¼ 12), and borderline signi /uniFB01 cant for Cu ( p < 0.054, n ¼ 12). Between sites, there were no signi /uniFB01 cant differences for MeHg and other trace elements (Mg, K, Mn, Zn, Cu, and Ni) in brown and white rice grain; however, HgT levels in brown rice were signi /uniFB01 cantly higher in site 3 compared to site 2 (ANOVA, p < 0.05, n ¼ 12) (Table 2).

Nutrients more concentrated in these layers are reduced during the milling process.

Unlike most other trace elements, milled white rice did not result in a reduction in MeHg levels. Variability for MeHg was also higher compared to other micronutrients, which possibly re /uniFB02 ected higher RPD between replicate digestions (MeHg: 24%; HgT: 12%; Ni: 27%, others: < 8%) (Table 1). Similar MeHg levels in white and brown rice grain suggested more ef /uniFB01 cient unloading of this species into the endosperm. In rice grain, the /uniFB01 lial tissue (endosperm, germ, and aleurone) is isolated from the maternal tissue (pericarp, placenta, vascular tissue, chalaza, and nucellus) (Krishnan and Dayanandan, 2003). The ovular vascular trace, which is part of the maternal tissue, is the only source of nutrients for the developing grain (Krishnan and Dayanandan, 2003), and is considered a bottleneck for nutrient unloading (Lombi et al., 2009). It is possible organic nutrients, including MeHg, utilize membrane transport pathways into the grain more ef /uniFB01 ciently, which was reported in rice grain for organic dimethylarsinic acid (Carey et al., 2010; Lombi et al., 2009; Meharg et al., 2008) and for organic selenium species (Li et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2010; Williams et al., 2009).

## 4. Conclusions

AWD water-saving methods did not affect the uptake rate (i.e., slope of the regression line) of HgT and MeHg between the soil and rice grain, although other factors may be important.

Despite drier, more aerobic conditions in the water-saving paddies, the uptake and translocation rates of HgT and MeHg from the soil to the rice grain were similar between three water-saving sites and one nonwater-saving site. Unlike other trace elements, MeHg concentrations were not signi /uniFB01 cantly reduced in milled white rice, which indicated MeHg in /uniFB01 ltrated the endosperm more easily than inorganic Hg(II). The latter is important, since polished white rice is the fraction ingested throughout Asia. This was an observational study, and more research is needed to understand the effect of watersaving irrigation methods on the bioavailability and uptake of trace elements, including toxic elements such as MeHg, from paddy soil.

## 3.3. Calculation of daily MeHg ingestion rate

The average rice ingestion rate in 2008 in China was 270 g/d, which was based on the annual total rice consumption (130,778 /C2 10 3 t, from IRRI, 2010) and the population of China (1,324,655 /C2 10 3 , from PRB, 2010).

Using the mean MeHg levels in white rice (average: 1.2 ng/g, n ¼ 12), and assuming mean body weight is 60 kg, the mean daily MeHg intake rate from rice ingestion was 0.0054 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 , which was 17 times lower than the U.S. EPA recommended level (0.1 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 , USEPA, 2001b). Higher MeHg exposure levels were reported for brown rice in the Hg mining area in China, assuming the daily rice ingestion rate was 620 g/d (e.g., 0.26 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 from Qiu et al., 2008; 0.012 e 0.44 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 from Zhang et al., 2010c). Using the higher ingestion rate, the daily MeHg exposure level for this study was 0.012 m g kg /C0 1 d /C0 1 (i.e., 8.1 times lower than the U.S. EPA reference dose, USEPA, 2001b), which indicated rice grain harvested from these paddies near Tuanlin village, Hubei province, China was not a signi /uniFB01 cant source of MeHg to humans.
